g.title: paper carefully ablates where stochastic anchoring should be applied
g.desc: The paper carefully ablates where stochastic anchoring should be applied.
g.text: Node features, an intermediate layer, or after readout?
The paper carefully ablates the placement of stochastic anchoring within the network.

g.title: D and D dataset most severe size shift applying anchoring after readout layer dramatically improves accuracy calibration network depth grows earlier-layer anchoring converges less well
g.desc: On the D and D dataset, which has the most severe size shift, applying anchoring after the readout layer dramatically improves both accuracy and calibration as network depth grows, while earlier-layer anchoring converges less well.
g.text: PREDICTIVE UNCERTAINTY UNDER SIZE SHIFT — D&D HAS THE MOST SEVERE SHIFT (Figure 4)
On D&D, anchoring after the READOUT layer dramatically improves both accuracy and calibration as depth grows,
whereas earlier-layer anchoring converges less well.

g.title: leads practical recommendation anchor last layer size-shift settings
g.desc: This leads to a practical recommendation to anchor at the last layer for size-shift settings.

g.title: authors also validate partial stochasticity pretrained variant only trains anchored classifier head effective scalable neural tangent kernel analysis confirms intermediate constant shifts truly alter model function not trivial reparameterization
g.desc: The authors also validate that partial stochasticity, in the form of the pretrained variant that only trains an anchored classifier head, is both effective and scalable, and a neural tangent kernel analysis confirms that intermediate constant shifts truly alter the model's function rather than acting as a trivial reparameterization.
g.text: The pretrained variant — training only an anchored classifier head — is both
effective and scalable. A neural tangent kernel analysis confirms that intermediate
constant shifts truly alter the model's function, not a trivial reparameterization.
